metadata.file_name: The Linkage between School Autonomy and Inequality in Achievement in 69 Countries  Does Development Level Matter .pdf
metadata.title: The Linkage between School Autonomy and Inequality in Achievement in 69 Countries: Does Development

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA microdata aggregated to a country-year panel for 69 countries across six PISA waves (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015). For each autonomy indicator, the authors compute country-year means weighted by PISA student survey weights, and then combine highly correlated indicators within autonomy domains using arithmetic means. For the first-stage estimation of SES gradients, they incorporate multiple plausible values for achievement and apply both student and school survey weights using Stata’s repest command, which is designed for complex survey/PV estimation. The paper does not train ML predictive models; instead it uses weighted mixed-effects regression, so survey weights are essential for representativeness and are explicitly applied rather than omitted.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Constructs a country-level panel using PISA 2000–2015 waves, including only countries/territories that participated in at least two PISA waves (yielding 322 country-waves). Excludes PISA 2018 because it does not contain the school autonomy measures used. For the analytic sample, the authors exclude missing values in the paper (noted as <10% for some variables), and they compute achievement inequality gradients separately for each country and wave before aggregating country-wave means of covariates. Development-level categories are fixed using World Bank classification in 2000, and the analysis focuses on lower-secondary age (15-year-olds) as represented in PISA.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2015 (15-year-olds), Mathematics achievement inequality by SES (country-wave panel; 69 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Maths achievement inequality (SES gradient) and school autonomy (pooled models)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted mixed-effects regression (country-wave panel; N-country-year=322; N-country=69). Reported as non-significant for all autonomy variables in Table 1 (p > .05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2015 the study leveraged academic autonomy, budget autonomy, hiring autonomy, and salary autonomy to predict maths achievement inequality (SES gradient) at the country-wave level, finding that the association between all autonomy variables and inequality in achievement was not significant in pooled analyses (p > .05). This indicates that implementing school autonomy reforms without context-specific equity safeguards may not reliably reduce SES-based achievement inequality, and effects may be heterogeneous rather than uniformly beneficial.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000–2015 (15-year-olds), Mathematics achievement inequality by SES (country-wave panel; 69 countries)
main_findings.target_variable: Moderation of autonomy effects by development level (interaction models)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Weighted mixed-effects regression with interactions (Table 2; N-country-year=322; N-country=69). Only academic autonomy interactions differ by development level in Model 8: Academic autonomy × upper-middle-income = 109.5 (p < .001) and Academic autonomy × high-income = 70.6 (p < .01); budget and personnel autonomy interactions are not significant. Variance explained by interaction terms ≈10% (vs 4 in non-interaction model).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000–2015 the study leveraged academic autonomy and its interactions with development level (2000), alongside budget and personnel autonomy, to predict maths achievement inequality (SES gradient), finding that academic autonomy is linked to increasing achievement inequality in high- and upper-middle-income countries but not in low- and lower-middle-income countries (academic autonomy × upper-middle-income: 109.5, p < .001; academic autonomy × high-income: 70.6, p < .01). This indicates that autonomy reforms may widen SES achievement gaps in more developed contexts unless accompanied by strong equity-oriented accountability and resource equalization mechanisms, while budget/personnel autonomy may not show the same development-dependent pattern.

data.outcome_summary: The study constructs a country-level panel using six PISA waves (2000, 2003, 2006, 2009, 2012, 2015) for 69 countries/territories, focusing on 15-year-olds’ mathematics achievement and estimating SES-based achievement inequality at the country-wave level. Achievement inequality is operationalized as the SES gradient on mathematics achievement, with plausible values incorporated via repest and weighted by student and school survey weights. In pooled weighted mixed-effects models (322 country-waves; 69 countries), none of the four autonomy domains (academic, budget, hiring, salary) shows a statistically significant association with inequality (p > .05). However, interaction models show that only academic autonomy differs by development level: academic autonomy × upper-middle-income (109.5, p < .001) and × high-income (70.6, p < .01) are significantly steeper than low/lower-middle-income groups, while budget and personnel autonomy interactions are not significant. The authors emphasize that results are robust to several specifications but cannot be interpreted causally due to potential endogeneity.
